t.2.3: There the trees, ever in flower, hum with maddened bees; the lotus-ponds, ever full of lotuses, wear girdles woven of rows of geese; the peacocks of that realm, their tails ever gleaming, lift their throats eagerly in cries; and the evenings, ever moonlit, are lovely, for the reign of darkness has been banished.
t.2.6: There, fanned by breezes cooled by the waters of the Mandākinī, their heat kept off by the shade of the mandāra trees growing along her banks, maidens courted by the immortals play at a game with jewels that must be searched for, hidden by fistfuls of golden sand thrown over them.
t.2.9: There, at midnight, moonstones hanging in nets of threads, struck by moonbeams made bright once you no longer block them, trickle clear drops of water and dispel the bodily weariness born of lovemaking in women whose embraces in their dearest lovers' arms have just been loosened.
t.2.12: In that city a single wish-granting tree brings forth every adornment women need: bright-colored garments, wine skilled in teaching the eyes their playful glances, bursting blossoms together with tender shoots, ornaments of every kind, and the red lac-dye fit for the lotus feet to tread on.
t.2.15: There, to the north of the palace of the Lord of Wealth, stands our house, recognizable from afar by its arched gateway, lovely as the bow of the Lord of the Gods. Near it grows a young mandāra tree, reared by my beloved as if it were her own son, its boughs bent low with clusters of blossoms within reach of the hand.
t.2.17: On the bank of that pond stands a pleasure-hill, its summit fashioned of lovely sapphires, delightful to behold with its ring of golden plantain trees; thinking, 'it is dear to my wife,' O friend, I look upon you with lightning flickering at your edges and, with an anxious heart, remember that very hill.
t.2.20: Good friend, keep these signs in your heart, and you will recognize it by them and by the conch and the lotus painted beside the door. Surely the house now has a faded luster because of my separation, for when the sun is gone the lotus does not keep its own beauty.
t.2.22: Slender, youthful, with teeth like jasmine buds and a lower lip like a ripe bimba fruit, slim at the waist, with eyes like a startled doe's and a deep navel, slow in gait from the weight of her hips and bending a little under her breasts, she who dwells there must be the Creator's very first creation in the realm of young women.
t.2.24: Surely the face of my beloved, its eyes swollen from violent weeping, its lower lip discolored by the heat of her sighs, resting on her hand and only partly visible because of her hanging locks, bears the wretchedness of the moon whose radiance is dimmed as you follow upon it.
t.2.27: Or she will be setting out on the ground, counting them with flowers laid at the threshold, the months that remain of the term fixed on the day of our parting, or savoring a union begun only within her heart; for such, as a rule, are the diversions of women separated from their beloveds.
t.2.30: Out of former love her eye went toward the moon's rays, cool with nectar, that had entered through the lattice window, and it turned back again just as quickly. Out of grief she covers it with lashes heavy with tears, neither awake nor asleep, like a land-lotus on a cloudy day.
t.2.35: When you draw near, I suspect that the eye of the doe-eyed one, its sidelong glances checked by her locks, bare of the gloss of collyrium, and, since she has given up wine, having forgotten the play of its brows, will throb in its upper part and take on the likeness of the beauty of a blue water-lily trembling as fish stir the water.
t.2.39: O you whose husband lives, know me to be the cloud, your husband's dear friend, come to your side bearing his messages laid up in my heart. With deep and tender rumblings I speed along the road the weary bands of travelers far from home, eager to loosen the braided hair of their women.
t.2.42: Dwelling far away, his path barred by hostile fate, he enters through those yearning imaginings your body with his own: your slender body with his wasted one, your burning body with his intensely burning one, your tear-drenched body with his tearful one, your ceaselessly longing body with his longing one, your hot-sighing body with his that sighs still more deeply.
t.2.45: Having painted you on a rock with mineral colors, angry from love, when I wish to draw myself fallen at your feet, just then my sight is blotted out again and again by welling tears; cruel Fate does not tolerate the union of us two even in that.
t.2.46: O young one, though I am already wasted thin, the five-arrowed god torments me, far removed as I am from this face of yours, fragrant like earth sprinkled by showers. Consider, now that the hot season is at its end, how could the days pass for me, when the sunlight is scattered by dense clouds spreading wide and clinging to every quarter of the sky?
t.2.49: How might the three-watched night, with its long watches, be shortened as if to a moment? How might the day too, in all its phases, have only the faintest heat? Thus, O restless-eyed one, my heart, longing for what is hard to attain, has been left without refuge by the fiercely burning pangs of separation from you.
t.2.51: My curse will end when Śārṅgapāṇi rises from his serpent couch; pass the remaining four months with your eyes closed. Afterwards the two of us will enjoy each and every one of our heart's desires, multiplied by separation, through nights bright with the moonlight of full autumn.
t.2.53: Knowing from the giving of this token that I am well, O dark-eyed one, do not let gossip make you distrustful of me. People say that affections somehow wither away in separation; but in truth, through lack of enjoyment, their longing for the desired one swells, and they become a very heap of love.
t.2.1: There, the palaces are fully able to rival you through their many distinctive features: you set graceful women trembling, while they hold lovely women; you bear the rainbow, while they are adorned with paintings; your thunder is deep and resonant, while their drums are struck for music; you carry water within, while their floors are made of jewels; and you are lofty, while their tops lick the clouds.
t.2.2: There the women hold a play-lotus in the hand and wear young kunda blossoms woven into their locks; the beauty of their faces is made pale with the pollen of lodhra flowers. In their braided hair they set fresh kuravaka, on the ear a lovely śirīṣa, and in the parting of the hair the nīpa blossom born of your coming.
t.2.4: There, where tears spring to the eyes from joy and from no other cause, there is no anguish but that born of the flower-arrowed god of love, which union with the beloved can cure. No separation arises except from lovers' quarrels, and for the lords of wealth there is surely no age other than youth.
t.2.5: There the Yakṣas, accompanied by the most excellent women, come to the terraces of their mansions made of white gems, adorned with flowers formed by the reflections of the stars, and enjoy the wine born of the wish-granting tree, whose fruit is love's delight, while drums deep-toned like your thunder are softly beaten.
t.2.8: In that city, clouds like you, led by their guide the ever-moving wind onto the topmost floors of its palaces, at once spoil the paintings there with drops of water, and then, as if seized by fear, slip out through the lattice windows, shredded into tatters, skilled at mimicking the puffs of smoke.
t.2.7: There, when lovers, their hands restless with passion, pull away the silken garments of the bimba-lipped women, already loosened by the untying of the waist-knot, the handful of powder flung by those women, bewildered with shame, is thrown in vain, for though it strikes the jewel-lamps with their tall flames full in front, it cannot put them out.
t.2.10: There, lovers with inexhaustible treasures stored within their mansions, accompanied by the foremost courtesans among the celestial women and absorbed in conversation, daily enjoy the outer garden called Vaibhrāja, together with sweet-throated Kiṃnaras who sing aloud the glory of the Lord of Wealth.
t.2.11: There, at the rising of the sun, the nightly path of the amorous women is betrayed by mandāra flowers fallen from their locks through the trembling of their hurried gait, by leaf-shaped ornaments and golden lotuses slipped from their ears, by nets of pearls, and by necklaces whose strings snapped against the swell of their breasts.
t.2.13: There the horses, dark as leaves, rival the steeds of the Sun; the elephants, lofty as mountains, rain ichor from their rut like you; and the foremost warriors, who stood in battle against Daśamukha, bear scars from the Candrahāsa sword that put the splendor of ornaments to shame.
t.2.14: Knowing that the god who is the friend of the Lord of Wealth dwells there in person, Manmatha, out of fear, mostly does not carry his bow strung with bees; his work is accomplished by the coquetries of clever women alone, whose glances, darted with knitted brows, never miss their targets, the lovers.
t.2.16: And in it there is a pond whose flight of steps is laid with slabs of emerald, covered with full-blown golden lotuses on stalks of glossy beryl; the swans who have made their dwelling in its water, free from sorrow, will not pine for nearby Lake Mānasa even when they see you.
t.2.18: Here, close to the mādhavī bower with its hedge of kuravaka, stand a red aśoka with trembling young shoots and a lovely kesara. The one, like me, longs for the left foot of your friend; the other, under the pretext of its flowering-craving, yearns for the wine of her mouth.
t.2.19: And in the midst of them stands a golden perching-pole topped with a crystal slab, bound at its base with gems that gleam like young bamboo, on which, at the close of day, sits your friend the blue-throated peacock, made to dance by my beloved with clapping hands made lovely by tinkling bracelets.
t.2.21: Swiftly taking on the slender form of a young elephant so that you may descend quickly, and seated on the lovely summit of the pleasure-hill I spoke of before, you should cast into the house the glance of your lightning's flash, its light dimmed little by little, like the flickering play of a row of fireflies.
t.2.23: Know her, sparing of speech, to be my second life, alone like a female cakravāka while I, her companion, am far away; I think that the young woman, her longing grown intense as these heavy days pass, has become changed in form, like a lotus plant blighted by the frost.
t.2.25: She falls first upon your sight, either busy with the offerings, or drawing my likeness, wasted by separation, as her heart imagines it, or asking the sweet-voiced myna in its cage, “Do you remember our master, O tender one? For you were his darling.”
t.2.26: Or, gentle one, you will find her with her vīṇā laid on her lap in its soiled garment, longing to sing aloud a song whose words she has composed around my name. Having somehow wiped dry the string wet with the tears of her eyes, she forgets again and again the modulation, though she herself had composed it.
t.2.28: By day, while she is occupied with tasks, separation may not torment her so; but at night, I fear, your friend suffers heavier grief with nothing to divert her. So that you may comfort her with my messages, look upon that virtuous one at midnight, sleepless and lying on the bare ground, as you stand at the window of the mansion.
t.2.29: You will see her wasted with anguish, lying on one side upon her bed of separation, like the slender form of the cool-rayed moon with only a single digit left, low on the eastern horizon. With hot tears she drags through that very night, now made long by separation, which once, spent with me in love-play as we desired, passed like a single moment.
t.2.31: You will surely find her blowing aside, with sighs that torment the tender bud of her lower lip, the lock of hair that hangs down to her cheek, rough from bathing in plain water, and longing for sleep, though the welling flood of tears leaves it no room, wondering how union with me might come to her, even if only born of a dream.
t.2.32: She, with her hand whose nails are uncut, again and again pushes away from the curve of her cheek the single braid, hard, uneven and painful to the touch: that lock which was bound on the first day of our separation, its garland cast aside, and which I am to unbind at the end of the curse, when my grief has melted away.
t.2.33: That frail woman, bearing her delicate body stripped of its ornaments and laid again and again, with grievous pain, upon the lap of her bed, will surely make even you shed tears of fresh water; for, as a rule, everyone whose inner self is tender becomes compassionate.
t.2.34: I know that your friend's heart is filled with love for me; for this reason I imagine her to be in such a state in this first separation. It is surely not the conceit of thinking myself fortunate that makes me talkative; all that I have said, brother, you will soon see with your own eyes.
t.2.36: And her left thigh, now bereft of the marks of my nails and made by the course of fate to give up its long-familiar net of pearls, that thigh, pale as the stem of a fresh plantain and accustomed at the close of love's enjoyment to the soothing strokes of my hands, will begin to quiver.
t.2.37: At that time, O cloud, if she should be enjoying the bliss of sleep, wait beside her, holding back your thunder, and be patient for just one watch of the night. Otherwise her close embrace of me, her lover somehow found in a dream, might suddenly come undone, the knot of her creeper-like arms slipping from my neck.
t.2.38: Having roused her with a breeze cooled by your own fine droplets of water, so that she revives together with the fresh clusters of mālatī buds, keep your lightning hidden within you and, steady, begin to speak with words of thunder to that proud lady as she gazes with unmoving eyes at the window where you rest.
t.2.40: When you have spoken thus, she, like Maithilī turning eagerly toward the son of the Wind, will look up at you with a heart swelling with longing, and having welcomed you with honor, will listen attentively to what follows, gentle one; for to women, news of a beloved brought by a friend is only a little less than union itself.
t.2.41: O long-lived one, at my word and to do a kindness to yourself as well, you should speak to her thus: "Your companion, dwelling in the hermitages of Rāmagiri, still alive though parted from you, asks, O helpless one, after your well-being; for to living beings, to whom misfortunes come so easily, this is the very first thing to be said."
t.2.43: He who, out of longing to touch your face, used to be eager to whisper in your ear before your friends even what might well have been spoken aloud, he, now passed beyond the range of hearing and unseen by your eyes, speaks to you through my mouth these words, composed by longing.
t.2.44: In the śyāmā creepers I see your body, in the glances of startled does your gaze, in the moon the radiance of your face, in the heavy plumes of peacocks your hair, and in the slender ripples of rivers the playful arching of your brows. But alas, O fierce one, nowhere in any single thing is there a likeness of you.
t.2.48: O virtuous one, I embrace those winds from the snowy mountain which, having just burst open the leaf-bud sheaths of the devadāru trees and grown fragrant with the flow of their sap, have set out toward the south, thinking that perhaps they may have touched your body before.
t.2.47: When the deities of the woodland see me stretching my arms out into empty space to clasp you in a fierce embrace, you whom I have somehow found in visions of my dreams, surely it is not seldom that their tear-drops, large as pearls, fall upon the tender shoots of the trees.
t.2.50: Indeed, reflecting much upon myself, I sustain myself by my own strength; therefore, O fair one, do not you too fall into utter despair. To whom has happiness come without end, or sorrow absolutely? One's condition goes down and goes up in the manner of a wheel's rim.
t.2.52: And he said further: Once, long ago, as you lay in bed clinging to my neck, you fell asleep and then woke suddenly, weeping aloud for some reason; and when I asked you again and again, you told me with a hidden laugh, 'Rogue, I saw you in a dream making love to some other woman!'
t.2.54: Having thus consoled your friend, whose grief is fierce in this first separation, return swiftly from the mountain whose peaks are torn up by the bull of the Three-Eyed One. With her words, which send a token of recognition and news of her well-being, you should sustain my life too, which droops like a jasmine blossom at dawn.
t.2.55: I trust, gentle friend, that you have resolved to perform this friendly service for me; I surely do not take your grave silence as a refusal. Even without a sound you give water to the cātaka birds when they beg for it, for the only answer the good give to those who entreat them is to accomplish what they desire.
